std::env::current_exe should work under masked /proc at Linux

current_exe() uses `/proc/self/exe` which means it does not support masked `proc`as noted at https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/rust-coreutils/tree/debian/patches/require-utility-to-be-invoked-at-matching-path.patch?h=applied/ubuntu/devel .

But it should support container, initramfs, etc...

It should be able to support it by getauxval (and maybe, faster than `/proc/self/exe`?).

For clarification, because it isn't a function I've ever used or was familiar with, this is referring to [`std::env::current_exe`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/env/fn.current_exe.html), and in particular the Linux implementation thereof:

https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/56aaf58ec02b6ac974e8364269fbb33a8a806e28/library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/os.rs#L265-L273

https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=002bef5b0ef8a232777289f057d7b860

They do not return the same value, `AT_EXECFN` is the literal path used to start the executable, while `/proc/self/exe` will be a symbolic link that can be resolved to an absolute path.

It looks like that when using a relative path to start the executable, `AT_EXECFN` will preserve this relative path. This means that while it will be readable at startup, it will no longer be accessible after the process changes its working directory.

Example:
```rust
fn main() {
    std::env::set_current_dir("/nix");
    dbg!(std::env::current_exe());
    dbg!(unsafe { std::ffi::CStr::from_ptr(libc::getauxval(libc::AT_EXECFN) as _) });
}
```
```
./path/main
[src/main.rs:3:5] std::env::current_exe() = Ok(
    "/tmp/scratchYbUWvz9ol/path/main",
)
[src/main.rs:4:5] unsafe { std::ffi::CStr::from_ptr(libc::getauxval(libc::AT_EXECFN) as _) } = "./path/main"
```

As such I don't think this is a good *replacement* for `/proc/self/exe`. At most it could be a fallback. But even then this behavior won't work very well, `current_exe()` is documented as
> Returns the full filesystem

But I guess it might be better than nothing?
How about recursing readlink for AT_EXECFN?

By the time the user runs `std::env::current_exe()` it is already too late to resolve `AT_EXECFN` to an absolute path. The working directory might have changed since starting the process. It is only usable by the dynamic linker or libc before any user code ran.

> But it should support container

Afaik pretty much every container implementation will mount `/proc`.

> initramfs

If you use systemd inside the initramfs, /proc will be mounted by systemd afaik. Alpine's initramfs generator mounts /proc too: https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/mkinitfs/-/blob/master/initramfs-init.in?ref_type=heads#L505 Same for Debian's version: https://salsa.debian.org/kernel-team/initramfs-tools/-/blob/debian/latest/init?ref_type=heads#L14 I guess for those you do have an issue if `mount` and `mkdir` are implemented by uutils though.

Note that this is not the only place where the rust standard library expects the standard mounts like `/proc` and `/dev` to be present. For example `/dev/null` must exist when any of the stdio fds are closed at startup: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/06cafcbe08b1b0d4235685abd5f817ae1979cefa/library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/mod.rs#L69 And on systems without `getrandom`, we need `/dev/urandom` when creating a hashmap. And the `Debug` impl for `File` uses `/proc/self/fd`. And on systems without `getauxval` we fallback to `/proc/self/auxv`. And `std::process::available_concurrency()` needs `/proc` and `/sys`.

> Note that this is not the only place where the rust standard library expects the standard mounts like `/proc` and `/dev` to be present.

At least with `/dev`, POSIX mandates its existence, and it specifically promises the existence of a special file `/dev/null`. Linux additionally promises that `/dev` contains some devices and special files (e.g. `/dev/zero` and `/dev/urandom`) that are not required by POSIX.

> as noted at https://git.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/rust-coreutils/tree/debian/patches/require-utility-to-be-invoked-at-matching-path.patch?h=applied/ubuntu/devel .

I'm getting a 404
In my memory, the linked patch compares `argv[0]` and `/proc/self/exe` for security. Panics if `/proc/self/exe` is unavaiable.

On a SaaS VM, kind of a limited VPS at *pythonanywhere.com*, I am trying to upgrade the private binary **uv** that I am using to setup my python venv:

```
$ uv self upgrade
error: no /proc/self/exe available. Is /proc mounted?
```
I think adding `std::env::start_exe` is making a sence. Current path is not needed in some case.

> By the time the user runs `std::env::current_exe()` it is already too late to resolve AT_EXECFN to an absolute path. The working directory might have changed since starting the process. It is only usable by the dynamic linker or libc before any user code ran.

In theory we could generate code before main runs that resolves `AT_EXECFN`. AFAICT this should be compatible with the current documentation of `std::env::current_exe()`.
duplcated

`missing_docs` is a lint provided by rustc instead of clippy. You should open this issue in rustc instead.
@eggyal You can check the linked repo. Some `#![expect(missing_docs)]` works on _some_ enum whose variants have no docs, but it reports false positive on `enum Value`.

Following the URL you gave to the failing GitHub action took me to the following:

https://github.com/fast/pqb/blob/e892ca657ac8d49c919dc6209337f754d4151251/pqb/src/value.rs#L24-L27

```rust
/// SQL value variants.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
#[expect(missing_docs)]
pub enum Value {
```

This `enum Value` does have some documentation (namely "SQL value variants."), so of course the `expect(missing_docs)` is unfulfilled.  Are there other examples?

I don't understand the problem.  You're telling the compiler that you expect there to be missing documentation, but in fact documentation is present.  The compiler is therefore alerting you to the failure of your expectation.  That is not a false positive.

Perhaps you intended to `#[allow(missing_docs)]` instead?

@eggyal What's the different between these two structures?

```rust
/// SQL keywords.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[non_exhaustive]
#[expect(missing_docs)]
pub enum Keyword {
    Null,
    CurrentTimestamp,
}

/// SQL value variants.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
#[expect(missing_docs)]
pub enum Value {
    Bool(Option<bool>),
    TinyInt(Option<i8>),
    SmallInt(Option<i16>),
    Int(Option<i32>),
    BigInt(Option<i64>),
    TinyUnsigned(Option<u8>),
    SmallUnsigned(Option<u16>),
    Unsigned(Option<u32>),
    BigUnsigned(Option<u64>),
    Float(Option<f32>),
    Double(Option<f64>),
    String(Option<String>),
    Array(Option<Vec<Value>>),
    #[cfg(feature = "with-json")]
    Json(Option<Box<Json>>),
    #[cfg(feature = "with-uuid")]
    Uuid(Option<Uuid>),
}
```

Clippy is OK fo `Keyword` but complains with `unfulfilled-lint-expectations` on `Value`. I would see both of them (1) having docs on enum type (2) no docs on variants.

My intention is to allow this pattern and `#[allow(missing_docs)]` works. But I'm confused with the different manner of `#[expect(missing_docs)]`.
Also, clippy doesn't complain with it on about nightly 2026-01-xx, but recently it fails.

Ah, I take back what I said before.  The variants themselves also need documenting, of course.  Therefore the `expect(missing_docs)` should indeed be fulfilled in both cases.

@rustbot label: -S-needs-repro +S-has-mcve

deliberation_thread.body:
This is multiple issues in one and probably makes sense to split things out. Right now it's somewhat hard to read.

At it's core, the difference between `for<'a> Ty:` and `for<'a> Ty: Trait` or `for<'a> Ty: 'b` is that with an empty lhs, we lower the where-clause to `for<'a> WellFormed(Ty). If not, we do not emit a well-formed goal.

A higher-ranked well-formed goal gets instantiated and we then prove well-formed for the instantiated types, resulting in errors due to missing implied bounds and generally detecting that things are not wf.

---

When checking that items are well-formed, we also test their where-clauses via https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/d34f1f931489618efffc4007e6b6bdb9e10f6467/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/wf.rs#L175

This then drops requirements if they contain any escaping bound vars https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/d34f1f931489618efffc4007e6b6bdb9e10f6467/compiler/rustc_trait_selection/src/traits/wf.rs#L603. This means we don't check anything for types if they reference a higher-ranked lifetime from the where-bound.

---

The same applies for trait objects, we don't check that their nested types are wf if they mention a higher-ranked lifetime from the trait object.

Longterm this will be fixed by @BoxyUwU's where-bounds on binders work.

I think separately tracking the ICE here would be good, as we might be able to do something about the before then

closing this as the first half is "intended" and the second one is actually an unsoundness tracked in #152489

gj uncovering this issue

deliberation_thread.body:
Regressed by #152287 cc @jakubadamw @petrochenkov

@rustbot label +A-dyn-trait +I-unsound -needs-triage

Neither looks like an MCVE to me 😅. Ideally we would add sth. nicer to Jubilee's revert PR.

Side note: Under the next solver this fails MIR validation:

```
error: internal compiler error: /rustc-dev/a423f68a0d75656eabab4982a06bed9f316f7109/compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/validate.rs:81:25: broken MIR in Item(DefId(0:14 ~ u_min1[bcc4]::main)) (after phase change to runtime-optimized) at bb0[1]:
                                Unsize coercion, but `&{coroutine@u_min1.rs:16:40: 16:42}` isn't coercible to `&dyn TraitA`
```

Under `RUSTC_LOG=debug` I could find the problematic call:

```
34ms DEBUG rustc_trait_selection::traits instantiate_and_check_impossible_predicates(key=(DefId(0:4 ~ u_min1[bc15]::TraitA::m), [Coroutine(DefId(0:15 ~ u_min1[bc15]::main::{closure#0}), [(), (), (), (), ()])])) = true
```

These two pieces of information aren't that insightful, I know. I'm just really annoyed that I can't get rid of the coroutine in favor a normal closure ^^'.
@fmease In my reproducer, I think that rust is confused on whether the async block implements Send or not. The problematic variable `_x` is being held across an await point.
I think this is related to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/110338

See also https://github.com/rust-lang/trait-system-refactor-initiative/issues/251

cc @lcnr

> [@fmease](https://github.com/fmease) In my reproducer, I think that rust is confused on whether the async block implements Send or not. The problematic variable `_x` is being held across an await point.

In both your and my reduced reproducers, the compiler ends up checking the same thing, namely whether `{coroutine@…}: Send` holds. async blocks desugar to coroutines, so there's nothing surprising. I literally copy/pasted the HIR expansion of the async block which is a coroutine.

Note the coroutine / async block is generally considered to impl `Send` by rustc (I guess that's correct?). It's just that prior to PR #152287 when checking if it's possible to omit the vtable entry for `TraitA::m` (`TaskFn::call_task`) due to trivially unsatisfiable bounds, we apparently used to check 0 predicates according to the logs but now we check whether `{coroutine@…}: Send` (that's the `G: Send` from the parent but instantiated) holds in an empty env which it doesn't (interestingly 🤔), so we omit `m` / `call_task`. Hmm, but yea it's unclear why the answers differ. After all `main`'s `ParamEnv` is also empty… Maybe the generic args (of the coroutine) differ or bound vars get instantiated differently?

LLVM says the optimized form's IR is
```llvm
; try_mcve_2026_2_16::main
; Function Attrs: mustprogress nofree norecurse noreturn nosync nounwind nonlazybind willreturn memory(none) uwtable
define hidden void @try_mcve_2026_2_16::main() unnamed_addr #3 personality ptr @rust_eh_personality {
start:
  unreachable
}
```
which is consistent with this reaching SIGILL.

I'm guessing that, whatever was checking whether the async block implements Send for the purposes of generating the vtable, it didn't see that the `make_none` function returned an `impl Send`, so it looked inside the `make_none` function and somehow concluded that the concrete type behind `impl Send` doesn't implement `Send`.

After a few initial passes, SROA and then EarlyCSE notices the program is bogus:

```diff
@vtable.0 = private constant <{ ptr, [16 x i8], [8 x i8] }> <{ ptr @core[57d357369df3eb5e]::ptr::drop_in_place::<example[e560b268c9334b1b]::broken::{closure#0}>, [16 x i8] c"\01\00\00\00\00\00\00\00\01\00\00\00\00\00\00\00", [8 x i8] undef }>, align 8

define internal void @core[57d357369df3eb5e]::ptr::drop_in_place::<example[e560b268c9334b1b]::broken::{closure#0}>(ptr noalias noundef align 1 dereferenceable(1) %_1) unnamed_addr {
start:
  ret void
}

define void @broken() unnamed_addr #0 personality ptr @rust_eh_personality {
start:
- %0 = alloca [16 x i8], align 8
- %dyn_a.dbg.spill = alloca [16 x i8], align 8
  %coro = alloca [1 x i8], align 1
  call void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr %coro)
  store i8 0, ptr %coro, align 1
- store ptr %coro, ptr %dyn_a.dbg.spill, align 8
- %1 = getelementptr inbounds i8, ptr %dyn_a.dbg.spill, i64 8
- store ptr @vtable.0, ptr %1, align 8
- %2 = load ptr, ptr getelementptr inbounds (i8, ptr @vtable.0, i64 24), align 8
- invoke void %2(ptr noundef align 1 %coro)
+ invoke void undef(ptr noundef align 1 %coro)
          to label %bb1 unwind label %cleanup

cleanup:                                          ; preds = %start
```

(the contents of `cleanup` don't matter after this.)

so as far as I can tell, we basically forget to generate some uhh *mildly important* parts of the coroutine and/or vtable.

After the merged revert, this is no longer a *critical*-level concern. I am leaving this open with the I-unsound and I-miscompile cases because this... well, what Ralf just added.

bgw (external):Miscompilation causing segfault with `dyn Future` on recent nightly versions This is the smallest possible reproduction I was able to come up with: ```rust use std::{any::Any, future::Future, pin::Pin}; trait TaskFn { fn call_task(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>>; } type Node = dyn Any; impl<F: Fn() -> Fut, Fut: Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static> TaskFn for F { fn call_task(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>> { Box::pin((self)()) } } trait Visit { type EdgesFuture: Send; } impl<VisitFn: Fn(&Node) -> EdgesFuture, EdgesFuture: Send> Visit for VisitFn { type EdgesFuture = EdgesFuture; } fn visit<V: Visit>(_: V) -> impl Future<Output = Option<V::EdgesFuture>> + Send { futures::future::ready(None::<V::EdgesFuture>) } fn main() { futures::executor::block_on( (Box::new(|| async { visit(|_: &Node| async {}).await; }) as Box<dyn TaskFn>) .call_task(), ) } ``` I expected to see this happen: Exit code zero Instead, this happened: `SIGSEGV` (or `SIGILL` if compiled in release mode) This can be reproduced in the rust playground by selecting the nightly compiler: https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=nightly&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=aaf6f4c5584fe181293b5f6cfbcd56de This example uses the `futures` crate, but this is a simply a minimal reduction of a bug I encountered with `tokio`. ### Meta This happens with any `rust-toolchain.toml` with a value equal to or newer than: ``` [toolchain] channel = "nightly-2026-02-10" ``` --- That translates to: `rustc --version --verbose`: ``` rustc 1.95.0-nightly (18d13b533 2026-02-09) binary: rustc commit-hash: 18d13b5332916ffca8eadb9106d54b5b434e9978 commit-date: 2026-02-09 host: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu release: 1.95.0-nightly LLVM version: 22.1.0 ``` --- This also reproduces on the latest nightly: ``` rustc 1.95.0-nightly (873b4beb0 2026-02-15) binary: rustc commit-hash: 873b4beb0cc726493b94c8ef21f68795c04fbbc1 commit-date: 2026-02-15 host: aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu release: 1.95.0-nightly LLVM version: 22.1.0 ``` This does not reproduce on any nightly releases older than what's shown here.
eggyal (contributor):Regressed by #152287 cc @jakubadamw @petrochenkov @rustbot label +A-dyn-trait +I-unsound -needs-triage
fmease (member):In-progress minimization (no longer depends on futures or crates other than `std`, still depends on coroutines tho): ```rs #![feature(coroutines, stmt_expr_attributes, yield_expr)] trait TraitA { fn m(&self); } impl<G: Send> TraitA for G { fn m(&self) {} } trait TraitB { type Ty: Send; } impl<F, T> TraitB for F where F: for<'a> Fn(&'a (dyn TraitC + 'static)) -> T, T: Send, { type Ty = T; } trait TraitC {} fn main() { let x: &dyn TraitA = &#[coroutine] || { let _x = g(|_: &_| {}); yield (); }; x.m() } fn g<T: TraitB>(_: T) -> impl Send { (loop {}) as T::Ty } ```
theemathas (contributor):A different minimization ```rust trait TaskFn { fn call_task(&self); } impl<Fut: Send> TaskFn for Fut { fn call_task(&self) {} } trait Visit { type Unit: Send; } impl Visit for for<'a> fn(&'a &'static i32) { type Unit = (); } fn make_none<V: Visit>() -> Option<impl Send> { None::<V::Unit> } fn main() { let _ = (&async { let _x = make_none::<for<'a> fn(&'a &'static i32)>(); std::future::pending::<()>().await; } as &dyn TaskFn) .call_task(); } ```
fmease (member):Neither looks like an MCVE to me 😅. Ideally we would add sth. nicer to Jubilee's revert PR. Side note: Under the next solver this fails MIR validation: ``` error: internal compiler error: /rustc-dev/a423f68a0d75656eabab4982a06bed9f316f7109/compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/validate.rs:81:25: broken MIR in Item(DefId(0:14 ~ u_min1[bcc4]::main)) (after phase change to runtime-optimized) at bb0[1]: Unsize coercion, but `&{coroutine@u_min1.rs:16:40: 16:42}` isn't coercible to `&dyn TraitA` ``` Under `RUSTC_LOG=debug` I could find the problematic call: ``` 34ms DEBUG rustc_trait_selection::traits instantiate_and_check_impossible_predicates(key=(DefId(0:4 ~ u_min1[bc15]::TraitA::m), [Coroutine(DefId(0:15 ~ u_min1[bc15]::main::{closure#0}), [(), (), (), (), ()])])) = true ``` These two pieces of information aren't that insightful, I know. I'm just really annoyed that I can't get rid of the coroutine in favor a normal closure ^^'.
theemathas (contributor):@fmease In my reproducer, I think that rust is confused on whether the async block implements Send or not. The problematic variable `_x` is being held across an await point.
theemathas (contributor):I think this is related to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/110338
theemathas (contributor):See also https://github.com/rust-lang/trait-system-refactor-initiative/issues/251 cc @lcnr
fmease (member):> [@fmease](https://github.com/fmease) In my reproducer, I think that rust is confused on whether the async block implements Send or not. The problematic variable `_x` is being held across an await point. In both your and my reduced reproducers, the compiler ends up checking the same thing, namely whether `{coroutine@…}: Send` holds. async blocks desugar to coroutines, so there's nothing surprising. I literally copy/pasted the HIR expansion of the async block which is a coroutine. Note the coroutine / async block is generally considered to impl `Send` by rustc (I guess that's correct?). It's just that prior to PR #152287 when checking if it's possible to omit the vtable entry for `TraitA::m` (`TaskFn::call_task`) due to trivially unsatisfiable bounds, we apparently used to check 0 predicates according to the logs but now we check whether `{coroutine@…}: Send` (that's the `G: Send` from the parent but instantiated) holds in an empty env which it doesn't (interestingly 🤔), so we omit `m` / `call_task`. Hmm, but yea it's unclear why the answers differ. After all `main`'s `ParamEnv` is also empty… Maybe the generic args (of the coroutine) differ or bound vars get instantiated differently?
workingjubilee (member):LLVM says the optimized form's IR is ```llvm ; try_mcve_2026_2_16::main ; Function Attrs: mustprogress nofree norecurse noreturn nosync nounwind nonlazybind willreturn memory(none) uwtable define hidden void @try_mcve_2026_2_16::main() unnamed_addr #3 personality ptr @rust_eh_personality { start: unreachable } ``` which is consistent with this reaching SIGILL.
theemathas (contributor):Relatedly, this code doesn't compile. (Note that `make_none` now returns an `impl Sized` instead of `impl Send`.) I think this ought to compile, since auto traits are supposed to work through `impl Trait` opaque types. ```rust trait Visit { type Unit: Send; } impl Visit for for<'a> fn(&'a &'static i32) { type Unit = (); } fn make_none<V: Visit>() -> Option<impl Sized> { None::<V::Unit> } fn foo() -> impl Send { async { let _x = make_none::<for<'a> fn(&'a &'static i32)>(); std::future::pending::<()>().await; } } ``` ``` error: implementation of `Visit` is not general enough --> src/lib.rs:14:5 | 14 | / async { 15 | | let _x = make_none::<for<'a> fn(&'a &'static i32)>(); 16 | | std::future::pending::<()>().await; 17 | | } | |_____^ implementation of `Visit` is not general enough | = note: `for<'a> fn(&'a &'0 i32)` must implement `Visit`, for any lifetime `'0`... = note: ...but `Visit` is actually implemented for the type `for<'a> fn(&'a &'static i32)` ```
theemathas (contributor):I'm guessing that, whatever was checking whether the async block implements Send for the purposes of generating the vtable, it didn't see that the `make_none` function returned an `impl Send`, so it looked inside the `make_none` function and somehow concluded that the concrete type behind `impl Send` doesn't implement `Send`.
workingjubilee (member):After a few initial passes, SROA and then EarlyCSE notices the program is bogus: ```diff @vtable.0 = private constant <{ ptr, [16 x i8], [8 x i8] }> <{ ptr @core[57d357369df3eb5e]::ptr::drop_in_place::<example[e560b268c9334b1b]::broken::{closure#0}>, [16 x i8] c"\01\00\00\00\00\00\00\00\01\00\00\00\00\00\00\00", [8 x i8] undef }>, align 8 define internal void @core[57d357369df3eb5e]::ptr::drop_in_place::<example[e560b268c9334b1b]::broken::{closure#0}>(ptr noalias noundef align 1 dereferenceable(1) %_1) unnamed_addr { start: ret void } define void @broken() unnamed_addr #0 personality ptr @rust_eh_personality { start: - %0 = alloca [16 x i8], align 8 - %dyn_a.dbg.spill = alloca [16 x i8], align 8 %coro = alloca [1 x i8], align 1 call void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0(ptr %coro) store i8 0, ptr %coro, align 1 - store ptr %coro, ptr %dyn_a.dbg.spill, align 8 - %1 = getelementptr inbounds i8, ptr %dyn_a.dbg.spill, i64 8 - store ptr @vtable.0, ptr %1, align 8 - %2 = load ptr, ptr getelementptr inbounds (i8, ptr @vtable.0, i64 24), align 8 - invoke void %2(ptr noundef align 1 %coro) + invoke void undef(ptr noundef align 1 %coro) to label %bb1 unwind label %cleanup cleanup: ; preds = %start ``` (the contents of `cleanup` don't matter after this.) so as far as I can tell, we basically forget to generate some uhh *mildly important* parts of the coroutine and/or vtable.
workingjubilee (member):After the merged revert, this is no longer a *critical*-level concern. I am leaving this open with the I-unsound and I-miscompile cases because this... well, what Ralf just added. @rustbot label: -P-critical -regression-from-stable-to-nightly
lcnr (contributor):That's a fun one. We fixed the unsoundness by reverting https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/152287. However, that PR was reasonable and should not have caused an unsoundness, so what's going on here. The core issue is the interation of https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/110338 with opaque types. When computing the witness type for coroutines we do not have region information available, so every occurance of a region is replaced with a unique bound region. ```rust trait Trait { type Assoc; } impl Trait for &'static u32 { type Assoc = (); } struct W<T: Trait>(T::Assoc); fn is_send<T: Send>(_: T) {} fn main() { // The witness contains `W<&'static u32>`. We don't know that // when computing the witness type and return `exists<'a> W<&'a u32>` // instead. // // To prove that the coroutine implements `Send` we need to show // `for<'a> W<&'a u32>: Send`, however, `'!a != 'static`, resulting // in an error when normalizing the field of `W`. is_send(async { std::future::ready(W::<&'static u32>(())).await; }); } ``` We can "preserve" the `W<&'static u32>: Send` proof by hiding it behind an opaque type: ```rust trait Trait { type Assoc; } impl Trait for &'static u32 { type Assoc = (); } struct W<T: Trait>(T::Assoc); fn prove_send_and_hide<T: Send>(x: T) -> impl Send { x } fn is_send<T: Send>(_: T) {} pub fn main() { // The witness is now `exists<'a> opaque::<W<&'a u32>>` // we never actually look into the opaque when proving // `opaque::<W<&'!a u32>>` during analysis, so this // coroutine does actually implement `Send`. is_send(async { let opaque_ty = prove_send_and_hide(W::<&'static u32>(())); std::future::ready(opaque_ty).await; }); } ``` However, this only works as long as we treat `impl Send` opaquely, if proving `Send` for it actually tries to look at its underlying type we get a higher-ranked region error. We look into opaque types during codegen, so checking whether this coroutine is `Send` there will emit a `'placeholder: 'static` region constraint again: ```rust //@ compile-flags: -Znext-solver //@ known-bug: trait-system-refactor-initiative#251 trait Trait { type Assoc; } impl Trait for &'static u32 { type Assoc = (); } struct W<T: Trait>(T::Assoc); fn prove_send_and_hide<T: Send>(x: T) -> impl Send { x } fn as_dyn_send(_: &dyn Send) {} pub fn main() { // Checking whether the cast to the trait object is correct // during MIR validation uses `TypingMode::PostAnalysis` and // therefore looks into the opaque. as_dyn_send(&async move { let opaque_ty = prove_send_and_hide(W::<&'static u32>(())); std::future::ready(opaque_ty).await; }); } ``` We do not check these region constraints outside of analysis, except in the *leak check* during trait solver. This means whether proving that the coroutine witness is `Send` fails after analysis depends on the specifics of whether we propagate region constraints and where we leak check. This differs between the old and new solver. In the old solver, `select` does not propagate constraints from nested `Trait` goals and also only uses the `leak_check` when doing candidate winnowing. While the old solver also adds this incorrect region constraint here, it never actually checks it and successfully compiles. The new solver does always propagate region constraints upwards, and also always uses the leak check at the end of every candidate. This means we're able to prove that the coroutine is `Send` during analysis, but not during codegen. **This was already unsound before https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/152287** as this can affect any use of `impossible_predicates`. That PR just made it easier to hit, as right now we only check this for specific vtable entries: ```rust trait Trait { type Assoc; } impl Trait for &'static u32 { type Assoc = (); } struct W<T: Trait>(T::Assoc); fn prove_send_and_hide<T: Send>(x: T) -> impl Send { x } trait ImpossiblePredicates<F> { fn call_me(&self) where F: Send, { println!("method body"); } } impl<F> ImpossiblePredicates<F> for () {} fn mk_trait_object<F>(_: F) -> Box<dyn ImpossiblePredicates<F>> { Box::new(()) } pub fn main() { let obj = mk_trait_object(async { let opaque_ty = prove_send_and_hide(W::<&'static u32>(())); std::future::ready(opaque_ty).await; }); // `call_me` is not a valid entry of the vtable as we consider // the coroutine witness to not implement `Send` during codegen. // This is UB. obj.call_me(); } ``` One way in which this issue is harder to trigger is that the only errors during codegen are due to the leak check. As the leak check does not currently consider `TypeOutlives` constraints, replacing the self type of the `Trait` impl with `T` and `T: 'static` avoids this issue: ```rust //@ compile-flags: -Znext-solver //@ check-pass trait Trait { type Assoc; } impl<T: 'static> Trait for T { type Assoc = (); } struct W<T: Trait>(T::Assoc); fn prove_send_and_hide<T: Send>(x: T) -> impl Send { x } fn as_dyn_send(_: &dyn Send) {} pub fn main() { // Checking whether the cast to the trait object is correct // during MIR validation uses `TypingMode::PostAnalysis` and // therefore looks into the opaque. as_dyn_send(&async move { let opaque_ty = prove_send_and_hide(W::<&'static u32>(())); std::future::ready(opaque_ty).await; }); } ```
lcnr (contributor):tracking the more general underlying unsoundness in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/153596

Given that it only happens on your computer and is spurious and the backtrace looks pretty odd I'm pretty sure that this is indeed a hardware issue. We get these reports from time to time, rustc is particularly fragile on broken hardware. It's entirely plausible that the rest of your system appears to work just fine.

It's likely bad RAM, but that's not the only possibility. Either way, I'm going to close this issue since it's almost certainly not a bug in Rust.
Bad SSDs/HDDs can fail/corrupt writes also, and the compiler does a lot of disk writing and reading.

We get these reports from time to time, rustc is particularly fragile on broken hardware. It's entirely plausible that the rest of your system appears to work just fine. It's likely bad RAM, but that's not the only possibility. Either way, I'm going to close this issue since it's almost certainly not a bug in Rust.
workingjubilee (member):Bad SSDs/HDDs can fail/corrupt writes also, and the compiler does a lot of disk writing and reading.

deliberation_thread.body:
`rustc_queries!` is very complicated

`rustc_queries!` is a proc macro at the heart of the compiler's query system. The call to it in `compiler/rustc_middle/src/queries.rs` defines all the queries. It's also **really** complicated. Until very recently, it produced five different things as output.

### `macro_rules! rustc_with_all_queries { .. }`
This is a higher-order macro. You can call it, passing it another macro which processes entries like this:
```
[(arena_cache)] fn registered_tools(()) -> & 'tcx ty::RegisteredTools,
```

### `macro_rules! rustc_feedable_queries { .. }`
Another higher-order macro, very similar to `rustc_with_all_queries`, but only including entries for feedable queries.

This was removed in #153009, hooray.

### `mod _description_fns`
A module containing one generated description function per query.

The body comes from the `desc` modifier. E.g. this modifier:
```
desc { "getting HIR ID of `{}`", tcx.def_path_str(key) }
```
gets turned into this function:
```
pub fn local_def_id_to_hir_id<'tcx>(tcx: TyCtxt<'tcx>, key: LocalDefId) -> String {                                              
    format!("getting HIR ID of `{}`", tcx.def_path_str(key))
}                                              
```

### `mod _cache_on_disk_if_fns`
A module containing one generated cache check function per `cache_on_disk_if` query.

The body comes from the `cache_on_disk_if` modifier, e.g. this modifier:
```
cache_on_disk_if { param.is_local() }
```
gets turned into this function:
```
pub fn const_param_default<'tcx>(_: TyCtxt<'tcx>, param: &crate::queries::const_param_default::Key<'tcx>) -> bool {                                    
    param.is_local()                           
} 
```

### `mod _analyzer_hints`
This is a weird module that exists purely to help rust-analyzer users find query definitions. It contains one never-executed function per query. E.g.
```
fn type_alias_is_lazy<'tcx>() -> bool {
    let crate::query::Providers { type_alias_is_lazy: _, .. };
    // These are the types in compiler/rustc_middle/src/query/modifiers.rs, just for documentation purposes.
    crate::query::modifiers::desc;
    crate::query::modifiers::separate_provide_extern;
    loop {}
}
```
The exact spans on the various identifiers are very important to get right.

### Summary

This one proc macro is doing a *lot*. It is incredibly hard to understand. I gained my understanding by `println!`ing the token stream and reading through things carefully. I don't know how else you could possibly understand it fully. It's clear that in the past people have modified it with only a partial understanding, leading to inconsistencies and weirdnesses, e.g. the inconsistent `tcx` binding syntax that was fixed in #152958.

The good news is that a lot of this functionality can be extracted from the proc macro and done instead in the declarative macros (e.g. `define_callbacks!`). Declarative macros are also not easy to read and understand, but they are *much* easier than proc macros. I think it should be possible to reduce the output from 2 macros + 3 mods down to 1 macro. (Though I'm not 100% sure about removing `mod _analyzer_hints`.) #153009 was a good start.
cc @Zalathar @oli-obk @cjgillot @Zoxc

In the past, I’ve run into several cases where I try to simplify some obviously-complex part of the query macros, but in the course of doing so I either break/degrade something important (which is why the complexity existed in the first place).

Or the alternative ends up being *more* complex or more subtle than what I started with, due to the awkward limitations of working with non-trivial `macro_rules!` macros, so it ends up not being worthwhile.

---

EDIT: To clarify, I’m not saying we shouldn’t try to improve or discuss the situation; my intent was to share my anecdotal experience of some things that make it tricky.

If it helps, think of this issue as me saying "I think the current situation is bad and I'm going to make it better if I can". It is *not* me saying "I think the current situation is bad and I'm definitely going to change it even if that makes things worse".

> Though I'm not 100% sure about removing `mod _analyzer_hints`

rust-analyzer does need these to be in the direct output of the proc macro.

> rust-analyzer does need these to be in the direct output of the proc macro.

So in summary, the rust-analyzer stuff is:
- Weird (generates special functions that are never executed and contains weird code, purely for r-a redirection purposes)
- Fragile (the spans have to be just right)
- Untested and possible untestable?

Not a good combination of characteristics!
@Veykril @ChayimFriedman2 is what exactly r-a needs here more... quantifiable?

I am guessing the thing r-a it "needs" is "rustc devs had a request and some odd hack was constructed and now we are changing our minds about what we want" but *probably* we can make this a strict improvement for both sides if the cleanup is complete enough.

Here's how I understand it:

- rust-analyzer can't possibly understand arbitrary macros, but it makes a best-effort attempt to map output tokens (which form normal Rust code that it can analyze) back to input tokens (in the macro call), to enable IDE features like hover docs and find-all-references on those tokens.
- There is a family of informal techniques that macro authors can use to guide r-a's best-effort mapping into giving more useful results, by carefully controlling how input tokens are used or not used, or by adding dummy uses of tokens in the right context to help guide the mapping.

(I don't think there's any specific collaboration between rustc and rust-analyzer here; it's just a particular instance of macro authors tweaking their macro to play nicely with r-a's macro handling.)

Yea the expansion there is chosen such that input tokens in the query macros map to those items with its spans allowing r-a to map to those, I've added that at the all hands last year to help people with the general issue of not being able to find the provider assignments easily as with this one can now at least see the assignments when doing a find all references. Its not great but was the best we could do with how the macro worked.
I couldn't get buy-in on eliminating `mod _description_fns` and `mod _cache_on_disk_if_fns`, and `mod _analyzer_hints` doesn't seem eliminable, alas. At least `rustc_feedable_queries!` is gone.

[(arena_cache)] fn registered_tools(()) -> & 'tcx ty::RegisteredTools,
```

### `macro_rules! rustc_feedable_queries { .. }`
Another higher-order macro, very similar to `rustc_with_all_queries`, but only including entries for feedable queries.

This was removed in #153009, hooray.

### `mod _description_fns`
A module containing one generated description function per query.

The body comes from the `desc` modifier. E.g. this modifier:
```
desc { "getting HIR ID of `{}`", tcx.def_path_str(key) }
```
gets turned into this function:
```
pub fn local_def_id_to_hir_id<'tcx>(tcx: TyCtxt<'tcx>, key: LocalDefId) -> String {                                              
    format!("getting HIR ID of `{}`", tcx.def_path_str(key))
}                                              
```

### `mod _cache_on_disk_if_fns`
A module containing one generated cache check function per `cache_on_disk_if` query.

The body comes from the `cache_on_disk_if` modifier, e.g. this modifier:
```
cache_on_disk_if { param.is_local() }
```
gets turned into this function:
```
pub fn const_param_default<'tcx>(_: TyCtxt<'tcx>, param: &crate::queries::const_param_default::Key<'tcx>) -> bool {                                    
    param.is_local()                           
} 
```

### `mod _analyzer_hints`
This is a weird module that exists purely to help rust-analyzer users find query definitions. It contains one never-executed function per query. E.g.
```
fn type_alias_is_lazy<'tcx>() -> bool {
    let crate::query::Providers { type_alias_is_lazy: _, .. };
    // These are the types in compiler/rustc_middle/src/query/modifiers.rs, just for documentation purposes.
    crate::query::modifiers::desc;
    crate::query::modifiers::separate_provide_extern;
    loop {}
}
```
The exact spans on the various identifiers are very important to get right.

### Summary

This one proc macro is doing a *lot*. It is incredibly hard to understand. I gained my understanding by `println!`ing the token stream and reading through things carefully. I don't know how else you could possibly understand it fully. It's clear that in the past people have modified it with only a partial understanding, leading to inconsistencies and weirdnesses, e.g. the inconsistent `tcx` binding syntax that was fixed in #152958.

The good news is that a lot of this functionality can be extracted from the proc macro and done instead in the declarative macros (e.g. `define_callbacks!`). Declarative macros are also not easy to read and understand, but they are *much* easier than proc macros. I think it should be possible to reduce the output from 2 macros + 3 mods down to 1 macro. (Though I'm not 100% sure about removing `mod _analyzer_hints`.) #153009 was a good start.

If the problem is caused by a rustc change, it's in this commit range: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/b3869b94cd1ed4bfa2eb28f301535d5e9599c713...859951e3c7c9d0322c39bad49221937455bdffcd.

I confirmed that https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/153079 (which reverts https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/152768) fixes our CI. Let's land that so we have time to figure out a proper fix without blocking Miri syncs.
I think I'm wrong re dynamic linking, we could do it on macOS too. But I _would_ want it measured and discussed separately.

cd rust
./x build library
....

  --- stderr
  llvm-config: error: libLLVM-22-rust-1.95.0-nightly.dylib is missing
```

I'm not sure how I can unblock my work. Do I need to build llvm from scratch?

Not sure what's happening there; https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/153079 only affects the dist builder, not your local builds.
Are you using download-rustc? Maybe that uses the dist artifacts and that's how it could be affected by this problem.

You could reset your rustc checkout to before the problem appeared:
```
# after saving your local diff
git reset --hard b3869b94cd1ed4bfa2eb28f301535d5e9599c713
```

Also somehow that PR that should fix this gets overtaken by tons of other PRs, we even had a huge rollup land (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/153116) before this regression fix... (and when it was in front of the queue of course github actions just broke :/ )

> FYI, I'm not clear, but this seems to completely break building rustc on macOS with the default developer settings:
> 
> ```
> git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/rust-lang/rust.git
> cd rust
> ./x build library
> ....
> 
>   --- stderr
>   llvm-config: error: libLLVM-22-rust-1.95.0-nightly.dylib is missing
> ```
> 
> I'm not sure how I can unblock my work. Do I need to build llvm from scratch?

That is https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/153127, I will take a look
UPDATE: that is not the same issue as this one.
UPDATE 2: ... but maybe root cause is the same?

Ah, finally. :)

@ZuseZ4  If you want to re-land that change, please do a `try jobs=dist-aarch64-apple` build and then ping me; I can check if Miri builds against that artifact.
I confirmed it now sort-of works, but due to https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/153146, if you don't have a shallow clone, it doesn't pick up the new hash. I don't know how to fix that.

     // the LLVM shared object file is named `LLVM-<LLVM-version>-rust-{version}-nightly`
```

Seems to be fixed by https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/153179, cache-busting LLVM did the trick.

Thanks @jieyouxu!

deliberation_thread.body:
Lang-nominating, since if-let guards are now stable in nightly, and is on its way to being actually stable on stable.

~~One possibility is destabilizing if-let guards only when used in combination with or-patterns.~~
I am quite confused because we do emit false edges for all these cases, so borrowck should not be seeing a difference between these cases.

As for what the correct behavior should be, I have two ideas.
- The current behavior.
- We make ref-for-guard bindings[^1] for by-move bindings assigned in `if let` guards if there's additional conditions, then move into the actual bindings for the arm if the whole guard succeeds[^2]. This would make `fails` compile, but it'd be an error to move out of a by-move binding later in the guard (similar to how you can't move out of the arm's pattern's by-move bindings in a guard).

I'm leaning towards keeping things as-is for simplicity. Notably, it's already possible to run into move errors in guards; as far as I can tell, `if let` guards are only unique in that bindings can be assigned after the guard succeeds. It matches against the left "branch" of the `_ | _` pattern, moves from `y` into `x`, fails the guard, then drops the `x`. It then matches against the right "branch" of the pattern, then attempts to move from `y` into `x` again, which isn't allowed. This makes sense. The `works2` function compiles. https://github.com/Pr0methean/rust_rdrand/tree/578e2c7a4375a39bbbbfe0e42088a58bf5e23f2c is a version that compiles and runs fine on x86_64 but still triggers SIGSEGV on aarch64.

This is just an LLVM assertion that fired. With `-Zverify-llvm-ir` you get

```
Intrinsic has incorrect return type!
ptr @llvm.aarch64.rndrrs
rustc-LLVM ERROR: Broken module found, compilation aborted!
```

It is expected that LLVM assertions cause a crash without any message. We compile LLVM with `-DLLVM_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS=OFF -DLLVM_UNREACHABLE_OPTIMIZE=OFF` which causes LLVM to turn every assertion into a trap, which in some cases is implemented as writing to an unmapped address: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/57f1ec6e0a4ec3cd4a485ca1ec85e3efe541933b/llvm/include/llvm/Support/Compiler.h#L488-L500 In addition it is very much expected that abusing LLVM intrinsics causes crashes when the LLVM IR verifier is disabled (as we do for perf reasons)

Your signature for that intrinsic is incorrect, based on the llvm test here 

https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/9cc615a2f5cfbdd28dc835758c35c12cba65e61f/llvm/test/CodeGen/AArch64/rand.ll#L22-L40

It should be 

```
declare { i64, i1 } @llvm.aarch64.rndrrs()
```

LLVM will segfault when you use an intrinsic with an incorrect type. 

---

Probably `rust-lang/stdarch` should wrap this intrinsic? Looks like it might be new in LLVM 22?
Does that translate to `fn rndrrs() -> (i64, bool)` in Rust, or to what?

For now this seems to work?

https://godbolt.org/z/41z84v18f

It might or it might not. Not all LLVM intrinsics can be called in Rust. For some there is no way to convince cg_llvm to lower Rust types to the right LLVM function signature. (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/140763 helps with that for a couple of types, but definitively not all) You will have to try. In any case, do note that the ability to call LLVM intrinsics is unstable and your ability to call any particular LLVM intrinsic may break without replacement in any future rustc version (in addition to the fact that LLVM occasionally changes LLVM intrinsics). `link_llvm_intrinsics` is effectively an implementation detail of stdarch. The `internal_features` lint triggers on it for a reason. If anything I would recommend using inline asm rather than an LLVM intrinsics for rndrrs.
@rustbot label -C-gub +C-discussion
Looks like adding it to `stdarch` is straightforward https://github.com/rust-lang/stdarch/pull/2050.
Closing as this is not-a-bug -- internal features are labeled "internal" for a reason. They should not be used outside this repository.

`#[doc = compile_error!()]` no longer emits a clean error

The following code used to only emit one error (the message passed to `compile_error!()`) on Rust 1.93, but on Rust 1.94, it emits both the given message and an unhelpful "attribute value must be a literal". 
```rust
#[doc = compile_error!("my error message")]
fn g() {}
```
[Godbolt link](https://godbolt.org/z/jne8s7Wbz).

I use this in [`doctest-file`](https://codeberg.org/Goat7658/doctest-file) to produce errors in a macro meant to be used in `#[doc = …]` position.

```rust
#[doc = compile_error!("my error message")]
fn g() {}
```
[Godbolt link](https://godbolt.org/z/jne8s7Wbz).

I use this in [`doctest-file`](https://codeberg.org/Goat7658/doctest-file) to produce errors in a macro meant to be used in `#[doc = …]` position.

HashMap::get has a footgun when using a different type for lookup

See https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html#method.get

> The key may be any borrowed form of the map’s key type, but [Hash](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/std/hash/trait.Hash.html) and [Eq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/std/cmp/trait.Eq.html) on the borrowed form must match those for the key type.

IMO, this requirement is so subtle that a documentation comment is not sufficient, we should aim to enforce this statically:

- The caller of `HashMap::get` has no way to know that two types have identical hash functions, since the hashing algorithm is in almost all cases an unstable implementation detail of the type, and even if it happens to match in one version, may not match in another version.

- There are legitimate reasons to need two "similar" types to hash differently (for example, interned strings may wish to hash themselves by hashing their address in memory, while also allowing the string contents to be borrowed with the Borrow trait, since hashing the address is much faster than iterating the string once the string is already interned)

- The consequences are dangerous: the code may appear to work fine in many cases, but may exhibit hard to debug logic errors, or catastrophic performance (say if the HashMap is used as a cache).

I would hope we can introduce a trait such as `HashCompatible<T>` that is implemented for all standard types. Obviously this cannot be added as a trait bound due to backwards compatibility issues, but a compiler warning could be introduced for when this bound is not satisfied, and this warning could be turned into a hard error in a future edition.
Isn't this precisely what `Borrow<T>` asserts, and what differentiates it from `AsRef<T>`—hence why it is used in `HashMap::get` etc?  How would the proposed `HashCompatible<T>` be any different?

FWIW I respectfully disagree with the premise: The quoted section of the docs do not establish said requirements just in passing; the method can only be called via a `Borrow<Q>` and a requirements for implementing `Borrow` are very clearly stated. If a type implements `Borrow` in a wrong way, it is 1) wrong everywhere, by definition, and can't be helped, and 2) is to be considered an API error not unlike a wrong `PartialEq`-impl. There is little one can do (although lints _do_ exists to spot obvious errors), and pushing this further down another abstraction layer doesn't solve the situation "If you lie here, remember, no refunds!" Afaics the second point ("interned string") does not even apply here, because a type that is 1) hashes differently than a string but 2) implements `Borrow` anyway is plain wrong according to pages and pages of documentation for `Borrow`; while `HashMap` is a dear customer of `Borrow`, the error is with the custom `impl Borrow` itself, not the `HashMap` type.

regression on nightly: queries overflow the depth limit

I last tested [this commit](https://git.filmroellchen.eu/filmroellchen/penplot/commit/6644b23f76639fca13e653fd191aab8a6082f112) in December 2025 with nightly 2025-12-04 (or thereabouts), which compiled. My specific command line was `RUSTFLAGS="-Z stack-protector=all -C link-arg=-Tlinkall.x -C link-arg=-Tdefmt.x -C force-frame-pointers -Z threads=20 " DEFMT_LOG="debug,esp_rtos=info,penplot=trace" cargo run -Z unstable-options -Zprofile-hint-mostly-unused --package penplot`, aka. with the parallel front-end.

After upgrading to nightly 2026-03-17, instead, the query recursion limit is hit here:

```
error: queries overflow the depth limit!
  |
  = help: consider increasing the recursion limit by adding a `#![recursion_limit = "256"]` attribute to your crate (`penplot`)
  = note: query depth increased by 130 when computing layout of `embassy_executor::raw::TaskPool<<() as web::web_task::_EmbassyInternalTaskTrait>::Fut, #[embassy_executor::task(pool_size = WEB_TASK_POOL_SIZE + WEB_TASK_POOL_SIZE_AP)]>`
```

From the existing issues, I assumed this was a parallel frontend bug, but that’s not the case, the same exact output happens with `RUSTFLAGS="-Z stack-protector=all -C link-arg=-Tlinkall.x -C link-arg=-Tdefmt.x -C force-frame-pointers" DEFMT_LOG="debug,esp_rtos=info,penplot=trace" cargo run --package penplot` as well (pretty much the minimal command line that shouldn’t change codegen).

Following the compiler’s suggestion fixes the issue and produces correct code.

It seems like this hasn’t been reported for embassy’s futures specifically, but GitHub’s search is not good enough for me to double-check. Apologies if this is a duplicate otherwise, as per the previous sentence I couldn’t find anything that’s quite exactly the same (also nothing that’s both still open and not only caused by the parallel frontend).
